OpenRouter is officially part of @stripe today!
More than 10 million developers and companies use OpenRouter, and as they build with more models across more workloads, they need control over what it costs and where their data goes.
OpenRouter has built that operating infrastructure to help run AI across every model and provider, with access to new models, uptime through outages, and enforced spend and data policies for each team.
Joining Stripe, which has spent years running critical infrastructure for businesses around the world, means we can build it faster and support companies at every scale.
Our commitment to neutrality stays the same. Models and providers compete on quality, reliability, and price. You decide what works for your business.
Stripe (@stripe)
OpenRouter is now part of Stripe.
Stripe is building the economic infrastructure for AI. Together with OpenRouter, we’ll help businesses explore new models and optimize token routing and usage.

Hugging Face + @OpenRouter:
Alex Atallah (@alexatallah)
Starting today, chat models on Hugging Face run through OpenRouter!
Open-weight models went from 27% to 72% of tokens on OpenRouter in under a year. A lot of that comes from two things: labs publishing their weights on Hugging Face 🤗, and dozens of providers competing to serve them on diverse dimensions.
Today we’re connecting the two. Chat models on the Hub now run through OpenRouter’s routing: 160 models from 38 labs, best provider picked per request, automatic failover, same HF token.
And your OpenRouter traces can now land in a Hugging Face bucket you own, ready for fine-tuning.
Excited to build this with @ClementDelangue, @julien_c, and the @huggingface team. More coming!

10/ I also went through the Antigravity logs to see how Neon actually works. 13 sessions on the XHigh setting, 762 tool calls in total:
- 313 file reads
- 266 edits
- 104 new files
- 43 shell commands
- 13 sub-agents
- 2 web searches
- 21 other calls, like task updates and questions to me
How it codes: every fix followed the same pattern. First it read all the files it needed at once (up to 16 in one go). Then it wrote the fix in one edit. Then it read the file again to check it. Each fix took roughly two to three minutes.
How it follows instructions: I told it 14 times to stay out of the terminal, and it ran zero shell commands in those runs. When I allowed it, it mostly started local web servers and ran its own checks.
How it delegates: for browser testing it sent out smaller Flash sub-agents to click through the demos. When those hit capacity errors, Neon asked me which model to try next. For the planet data it searched NASA and JPL directly.
Tokens: around 71M input over the day, 93% of it from cache, plus 1.8M output. There's no public pricing yet, so I can't tell you what all this costs.
The weak spot was capacity. The logs show 57 "no capacity" errors, and 4 runs just stopped and I had to restart them. Could be pre-launch load, but it cost me time.
My take: great for prototypes and solid code fixes. Expect some follow-ups.

10/ また、Neon が実際にどのように機能するかを確認するために反重力ログも調べました。 XHigh 設定で 13 セッション、合計 762 回のツール呼び出し:
- 313 ファイル読み取り
- 266 件の編集
- 104 個の新しいファイル
- 43 のシェルコマンド
- 13 人のサブエージェント
- ウェブ検索 2 回
- 他に 21 件の電話（タスクの更新や私への質問など）
コードの作成方法: すべての修正は同じパターンに従いました。まず、必要なすべてのファイルを一度に読み取ります (一度に最大 16 個)。その後、1 回の編集で修正が書き込まれました。次に、ファイルを再度読み取って確認します。各修正にはおよそ 2 ～ 3 分かかりました。
指示にどのように従うか: 端末にアクセスしないように 14 回指示しましたが、その実行ではシェル コマンドはまったく実行されませんでした。これを許可すると、主にローカル Web サーバーが起動され、独自のチェックが実行されました。
委任方法: ブラウザーのテストでは、デモをクリックするために小規模な Flash サブエージェントを送信しました。これらが容量エラーに遭遇すると、Neon は次にどのモデルを試すべきかを私に尋ねました。惑星データについては、NASA と JPL を直接検索しました。
トークン: 1 日で約 7,100 万の入力、その 93% がキャッシュから、さらに 180 万の出力。まだ公開価格が設定されていないため、これにかかる費用がいくらになるかはわかりません。
弱点は容量でした。ログには 57 件の「容量なし」エラーが表示され、4 件の実行が停止したため再起動する必要がありました。起動前のロードかもしれませんが、時間がかかりました。
私の意見: プロトタイプと確実なコード修正に最適です。続報を期待してください。

I’m deeply disappointed in our board
Bill Ackman (@BillAckman)
I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties.
What we know is that the board fired Jensen or forced his resignation for violating company policy and/or in response to the accusation of an affair with a spy.
They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders.
They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts.
How do we know this?
We know this by how quickly Jensen was fired and how little was known at the time of his firing.
It takes time to convene a board meeting. There was time, maybe, for one Zoom.
And this is a decision that should have been made by a board sitting in person and carefully deliberating the facts once they are known.
And they should have slept on the decision and met again the day after to discuss the facts, the risks and the other implications of their decision.
The timing and lack of information did not allow for careful board deliberation.
While boards can fire a CEO for an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, it should not be an automatic decision. That is why we have boards comprised of humans and not agents.
A board should consider whether or not such a relationship was consensual or whether it was an abuse of power dynamics. And a board has to consider what the impact of the firing is on all stakeholders.
If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment based on articles in the media. I would have made sure the board had all of the facts so it could make a careful and informed decision.
Boards of Delaware companies have a duty of care which means they must make informed, prudent and good faith decisions. This clearly did not happen here.
What law firm is advising this board?
Or is the board even taken good legal advice?
It doesn’t look like it.
And now the board is compounding its failures by insisting that there is no possibility for Jensen’s return as CEO.
Why is it in the best interest of the company to foreclose the possibility of Jensen’s return and to do so before all of the facts are known? This is yet another breach of their duty of care.
Furthermore, the board has launched an investigation whose scope is unknown. Investigations can be extremely damaging to a company and should be carefully targeted to address whatever facts need to be known rather than be overly broad in scope.
In short, this looks like a series of major governance failures by directors that panicked due to headlines in the media. They likely felt compelled to do something because they were afraid of looking bad in the media, not because it was the right thing for them company.
They couldn’t stand the heat.
The board’s conduct here is shocking for a company of this scale and importance to our country and the world at large, particularly at this moment in history.

ビル・アックマン (@BillAckman)
